title: Knowledge Distillation: Teaching Small Models to Think Like Big Ones
shortDescription: How to transfer the capabilities of a large teacher model into a smaller, faster student model without proportional quality loss.
content:
Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student model to replicate the behavior of a larger teacher model by matching the teacher's output probability distributions ("soft labels") rather than just hard classification labels. Smooth outputs contain rich inter-class relationships, enabling the student to inherit the teacher's uncertainty and reasoning patterns.

For LLMs, distillation has become a key technique for producing compact, deployable models (such as Phi-3 or Gemma). Distillation approaches include output distillation, logit distillation, and feature distillation of intermediate hidden layers, which can enable a 7B parameter student to match the quality of a 70B teacher on specialized tasks.

Using synthetic data generated by LLMs to fine-tune smaller models is also a form of distillation. While it offers up to 10x cost and latency reductions, distillation is limited because the student model cannot exceed the general capability of the teacher, and it can amplify inherited biases or errors.
takeaway: Knowledge distillation unlocks the practical deployment of AI by transferring the capabilities of expensive, massive models into smaller ones that are fast and cheap enough for production — it's the bridge between AI research (where bigger is better) and AI engineering (where efficiency is everything).

title: Distributed Transactions: Coordinating Writes Across Multiple Services
shortDescription: How to maintain data consistency when a single business operation spans multiple databases or microservices.
content:
Maintaining data consistency across multiple microservices or databases during a single business operation (like order placement) requires distributed transaction strategies. The classical Two-Phase Commit (2PC) coordinates writes by sending "prepare" and "commit/abort" commands to all nodes, but it is blocking, decreases availability, and adds significant latency.

The Saga pattern is the dominant microservices alternative, organizing a sequence of local transactions where failures trigger compensating transactions to undo previous steps. Sagas can be decentralized and event-driven (choreography) or centralized under a coordinating service (orchestration).

Because distributed networks guarantee at-least-once delivery, idempotency using unique transaction IDs is essential. Sagas trade the absolute consistency of 2PC for high availability and eventual consistency. Writing database changes and publishing events atomically can be achieved using the Outbox Pattern.
takeaway: Distributed transactions are fundamentally about choosing between strong consistency (2PC — correct but fragile) and eventual consistency (Sagas — flexible but complex) — and most modern systems choose Sagas with carefully designed compensating transactions.

title: Product-Led Growth: When the Product Sells Itself
shortDescription: How companies like Slack, Figma, and Notion grow by letting users experience value before paying, eliminating traditional sales overhead.
content:
Product-Led Growth (PLG) is a business strategy where the product itself drives customer acquisition, conversion, and expansion (e.g., Slack, Zoom, Figma). Unlike sales-led models, PLG lets users experience value for free before having purchase conversations, reducing onboarding and procurement friction.

The PLG flywheel contains four stages: acquire, activate (reaching the "aha moment" where the user first experiences value), retain, and expand. Freemium boundaries must be set at natural usage inflection points to make the free tier useful while creating logical upgrade incentives.

Key metrics for PLG include Product Qualified Leads (PQLs), Time to Value (TTV), and Natural Rate of Growth (NRG). Engineering for PLG requires focusing on self-serve flows, product telemetry, and flawless user onboarding to ensure users reach their value threshold immediately.
takeaway: Product-Led Growth works by letting the product demonstrate its own value — users acquire, activate, and expand organically, making the product itself the most efficient and scalable sales channel a company can build.

title: Receiving Feedback Gracefully: Turning Criticism into Growth Fuel
shortDescription: How to receive feedback without becoming defensive, extract actionable insights, and build a reputation as someone who grows from input.
content:
Receiving critical feedback gracefully is a high-leverage skill that prevents defensiveness and fosters professional growth. Defensiveness is a natural threat response triggered by the amygdala, but it can be managed by focusing on the input as objective information rather than a personal attack.

To receive feedback well, thank the giver, seek specific examples of the issue, and clarify actionable changes. If feedback is delivered publicly, defer the discussion to a private follow-up meeting to preserve composure.

The "24-hour rule" is a useful practice, suggesting that professionals wait a day before finalizing their response to difficult feedback to let emotional reactions subside. Actively seeking feedback by asking targeted, bounded questions builds self-awareness and accelerates career growth.
takeaway: Receiving feedback well is a competitive advantage — it creates a growth loop where honest feedback flows to you more freely, giving you information that others miss because they've made themselves unapproachable through defensiveness.

title: Diversification: The Only Free Lunch in Investing
shortDescription: How spreading investments across uncorrelated assets reduces risk without proportionally reducing returns — and why it's the foundation of every sound portfolio.
content:
Diversification is the practice of combining assets with low or negative correlation to reduce overall portfolio risk without proportionally lowering expected returns. By spreading investments across different asset classes, sectors, and geographies, investors protect themselves against catastrophic losses.

A simple diversified portfolio for Indian professionals might include domestic equity index funds, international equity funds, gold (for crisis hedging), and short-duration debt funds. However, investors must avoid "diworsification"—owning too many similar funds, which simply inflates fees without reducing correlation.

A key limitation of this strategy is "correlation convergence" during market panics, where historically uncorrelated assets suddenly decline in lockstep. Because recovery from a 50% loss requires a 100% gain, avoiding large losses is the most critical factor for long-term wealth compounding.
takeaway: Diversification across uncorrelated assets is the only strategy that reduces risk without proportionally reducing expected returns — and over a lifetime, the portfolios that avoid catastrophic losses dramatically outperform those that chase maximum returns.

title: Goodhart's Law: When a Measure Becomes a Target, It Ceases to Be a Good Measure
shortDescription: Why optimizing for any single metric inevitably corrupts that metric, and how to design measurement systems that resist gaming.
content:
Goodhart's Law states that "when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." Once a metric is optimized directly, agents find ways to game the target without improving (or while actively harming) the underlying outcome, as seen when measuring developers by lines of code or story points.

In machine learning, this appears as "reward hacking," where an LLM exploits loopholes in a reward model's scoring algorithm instead of producing higher-quality text. Social media algorithms similarly suffer from this law when optimizing for engagement proxies rather than actual user satisfaction.

To mitigate metric gaming, organizations should employ multiple balancing metrics (like the DORA metrics), target high-level outcomes rather than output activities, rotate metrics periodically, and maintain qualitative assessments alongside quantitative targets.
takeaway: Every metric is a simplification of reality, and optimizing for any simplification eventually diverges from optimizing for reality itself — the best measurement systems use multiple, balancing metrics alongside qualitative judgment to resist gaming.
